en: The First Fascicle of the *Vajrasattva-bhāṣita-pināyakadeva-siddhi-vidhi-sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
Translated by the Imperial Subject Dharma-bhadra, the Great Master Mingjiao, by imperial decree. At that time,
Vajrasattva spoke this supreme, foremost ritual manual,
which is capable [of benefiting] all sentient beings.
One performs various deeds for accomplishment and benefit;
even rites such as pacifying, increasing, magnetizing, and subjugating are all accomplished without exception.
What do you think?
This secret essential dharma-gate of the Great Vajrasattva possesses great majestic power;
if one applies oneself with a sincere mind according to the ritual, one will certainly attain accomplishment.
Vajrasattva said:
"If a vidyādhara wishes to subdue a śatru,
he should fashion an image of the deity Pināyaka."
Apply mustard oil to that image of the deity.
Using a cord made of wool,
tie it around the neck of the image.
The Vidyādhara, remaining naked,
suspends the image of that deity upon a wooden frame and burns it over a funeral pyre,
roasting the image.
One should then recite the Great Mantra while invoking the name of Śatru,
performing the rite from noon until sunset;
thus, that enemy will swiftly be bound and subdued.
Whatever one intends shall accord with the practitioner's wishes; if they wish to cease [the practice],
they may remove the celestial image and return to their usual state,
then use the previous image once again.
Soak it thoroughly with the milky sap of the nyagrodha tree,
and then apply the milky sap of the ariṣṭa tree to that divine image.
One should then recite the Great Mantra and invoke the name of Śatru; before long, that enemy will swiftly suffer from scabies and leprosy.
If one wishes to eliminate the illness, one should use fermented grain-water (yāsa) to wash the body of the image clean.
Anoint it with clarified butter, burn agalloch incense, and fumigate the image of that deity; one will quickly recover from illness.
Furthermore, for the rite of accomplishment:
fashion an image of the deity Pināyaka using nimba wood.
The deity is three finger-widths tall, with two arms and three eyes;
its hair is bound in a topknot adorned with a crown, and it sits upon a lotus flower, moist and radiant.
Wrap this divine image in a cloth used for childbirth.
When about to enter the temple of Maheśvara,
one should suspend [the effigy] from the top of a banner-pole using a rope;
the mantra-holder shall then call out the person's name.
Having thus recited the Great Mantra,
that person will swiftly depart from their native land and not return home again for even a hundred years.
From the beginning until the end of life,
if one wishes to cause [the deity] to return,
one should wash that celestial image with ghee and honey, and it will immediately become as it was before.
Furthermore, using the aforementioned image,
the vidyādhara first performs visualization according to the teachings of Avalokiteśvara;
thereafter, he applies powdered madhuka flowers to the body of the celestial image.
Furthermore, having combined poison, mustard seeds, salt, *mandārava* flowers,
and so forth into a single mixture, one should burn it as incense before the image and then bury it within a *dhruva* house or in the midst of that village.
The Vidyādhara should then recite the Great Mantra.
That Śatru will become utterly bewildered in body and mind;
if one wishes to rescue him, one should bathe that image with pure vajra water.
It will immediately become as it was before.
Then, using the previous image,
the vidyādhara proceeds to the temple of Maheśvara.
Dig a pit and bury him face-down within it.
Then, recite the Great Mantra while invoking the name of Śatru;
he will immediately become mute.
If one wishes to rescue them,
one should remove the celestial image; they will then return to their former state,
and one may again employ the previous image.
Take sesame seeds, non-glutinous rice, and leaves of the *nimba* tree;
place them together in wine and grind them finely.
Then, smear this upon the image of that deity.
Sprinkle it with the five kinds of pure water to purify it;
tie a cord made of hair to the celestial image and proceed to an empty house.
The Vidyādhara, naked and with disheveled hair,
recites the Great Mantra while uttering the person's name,
and uses his left hand to pull at the image of the deity.
That piśāca will swiftly be bound;
with shackles upon his body, he will experience great terror.
If a person performs the rite in this manner, [the result shall be as described].
Even Śakra, Lord of the Devas, would need to be struck with awe and fear;
how much more so for ordinary people?
If one wishes to bring it to rest:
Sprinkle wine upon the image, and it shall return to its former state.
Then, using the previous image,
wrap its body with birch bark.
The Vidyādhara went to the residence of that rāja from within his secret treasury-body and obtained great offerings, wealth, treasures, and so forth.
If one constantly wears it upon the body in secret and maintains its practice every day,
then wherever one walks, comes, or goes, one will be like one carrying a royal decree;
all who see one will treat them with reverence, attend to them, and make offerings.
Furthermore, using the aforementioned image,
on the eighth day of the waxing moon, one should receive the samaya-dharma before the celestial image in accordance with the original rite.
Having made offerings of food and drink,
the vidyādhara should place his left knee on the ground, join his palms in homage,
and recite the great mantra to seek the accomplishment of all matters according to his wishes.
When the practitioner thus bears the celestial image upon his head and enters into the presence of the Rājagṛha,
that king and his retinue [will be affected].
One should gaze upon him with reverence, giving rise to great respect and affection.
Furthermore, as for the ritual for accomplishment:
one should fashion an image of the deity Pināyaka using wood from a funeral pyre.
He is twelve finger-widths tall, with two arms and three eyes.
He wears a crown upon his head and adorns his body with skulls;
he bites his lip with his teeth, manifesting a wrathful expression.
He wears human skin as clothing;
his right hand holds a sharp sword, and his left hand forms the *kṛkāṭaka* mudrā.
Furthermore, he uses a garland of withered *bilva* flowers to encircle the body of the celestial image.
The vidyādhara should smear his own body with the ashes of a corpse.
At the head of his bed,
he should construct a maṇḍala using mahā-ṛkṣa (great jackal) [hair/flesh].
When burning mahā-maṃsa incense and reciting the great mantra,
that celestial being will appear before one.
The vidyādhara offers arghya and wine;
the celestial beings, filled with joy, immediately proclaim matters of the past, future, and present.
The practitioner then declares: "Let a severe illness befall such-and-such a person."
Having spoken thus,
within three days he will contract a disease;
even [if he attempts] killing, dispatching, summoning, or subjugating [the victim].
Whatever the practitioner desires shall be accomplished.
If one wishes to bring it to rest,
smear the image with clarified butter and burn agalloch incense as an offering.
It will then return to its former state.
Furthermore, using the previous image, one should dig a pit in the ground knee-deep and bury it with the face of the image pressed against the bottom.
The vidyādhara shall wear yellow garments and a yellow shoulder-strap;
while reciting the great mantra and invoking the name of Śatru,
all the people of that village will engage in combat.
If one wishes to bring it to rest,
take out the celestial image and the battle will cease of its own accord.
Then, use the aforementioned image and place it atop the banner-pole at the tavern.
If a person sees that banner from afar, all their liquor will be ruined.
The mantra-holder should write the person's name upon the flagpole,
take it with him, and walk through the village in succession.
Wherever the staff reaches, the wine is all ruined.
If one wishes to stop this, one should use the horn of a black ram to wash the celestial image;
it will then return to its former state.
If one desires to find a beautiful young girl,
one should bury an image of that deity at the girl's door;
thereafter, that girl will not wish to marry anyone else.
Furthermore, using the aforementioned image,
one should smear the image of that deity with mustard oil and roast it over a fire of *khadira* wood fueled by funeral pyre embers.
At that time, the maiden will suffer from a high fever and dream of marrying that man.
The practitioner bathes the image with milk and thereby attains accomplishment.
Furthermore, using the aforementioned image, one ties it with a rope made of kuśa grass and places it inside a cowshed.
If one drags them with a rope,
all the cattle will fall ill.
To cease this, one should fill a vessel with milk.
The statue was restored to its original state within the shrine.
Furthermore, using the previous statue,
he tied it with ropes and led it through the marketplace.
All the people of the marketplace stripped themselves naked,
let their hair down, and performed a dance;
they then used the aforementioned image.
The vidyādhara holds [the vessel] secretly with his left hand.
Upon seeing a woman carrying water,
he himself performs a dance, spinning in circles.
She saw him naked, carrying water and performing a dance;
this continued for two months.
Whenever she wished to cease, she would bathe the image with water.
It will immediately return to its original state.
Then, take the previous image and wrap it in a shroud from a corpse,
and roast it over a funeral pyre.
If one utters the person's name and recites the Great Mantra (mahāvidyā),
that person will swiftly contract a grave illness from which no one can save them.
However, if one bathes a celestial image with pure vajra-water, [the affliction will be removed].
He shall immediately be restored to health.
Furthermore, regarding the method for accomplishment:
the vidyādhara should use khadira wood.
He is fashioned in the image of the deity Pināyaka,
with four faces and eight arms;
his first right hand holds a sharp sword.
The second hand holds a battle-axe;
the third hand holds a vajra;
the fourth hand holds an arrow.
The first left hand holds a trident;
the second hand holds a kīṭaka;
the third hand holds a narmaruṅka.
The fourth hand holds a bow.
Having fashioned the image in this manner,
at the time when two armies engage in combat, [one should recite].
By bathing the celestial image with water, the battle will cease of its own accord.
Furthermore, using the aforementioned image and powder made from khadira wood,
one should smear that celestial image.
Boil that divine image with the milk of a black goat,
while reciting the Great Mantra and announcing the matter for which one seeks success.
Then, that divine image [will manifest] before all the people of the cities and villages.
All [the deities] appeared in dreams, saying:
"A certain vidyādhara has now come to this place;
you should welcome him, pay him respect, and make offerings to him."
Having spoken thus, they all welcomed him and made offerings according to the Dharma.
Then, using the aforementioned image and the roots, branches, and leaves of radishes,
they ground them into a paste like mud and smeared it over that celestial image.
Furthermore, by soaking that celestial image in gruel-water and reciting the Great Mantra,
one will attain the respect and affection of all Brahmins.
Furthermore, using the aforementioned image along with sesame flour, white non-glutinous rice, and *nerīva* grass,
one should mix them together like clay and smear it over the image of that deity.
Then, one should roast it over a fire fueled by *prāśa* wood.
He then recited the Great Mantra.
Consequently, the kṣatriyas, kings, and others all conceived feelings of reverence,
affection, and respect, and offered him worship.
Furthermore, using the aforementioned image,
smear it with granulated sugar and roast it over a fire while reciting the Great Mantra.
Then, fumigate it with the smoke of fish.
One will immediately gain the respect and affection of Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others.
Furthermore, for the rite of accomplishment,
one should use wood from a parasitic tree growing upon a nimba tree.
One should fashion an image of the deity Pināyaka,
the size of a thumb,
with four arms and three eyes.
The first right hand holds a sharp sword;
the second right hand holds a battle-axe;
the first left hand holds a noose.
In his second hand he held a ball of *saṃmodana* food;
as a snake formed a sling around his armpit, a thousand fangs protruded from his mouth.
Having done this, [he stood there].
Using black bean flour as a paste, coat the image of that deity.
Having recited the Great Mantra,
secretly bury this image in front of another person's door.
All those with two feet, four feet, and so forth, who perceive signs of great evil—
trampling, kicking, and causing terror— cannot be restrained by anyone;
yet when a Vidyādhara obtains great wealth and profit, they immediately come to a halt.
Furthermore, having empowered the aforementioned image with mantras,
the vidyādhara shall secretly bury it outside the monastery gate,
causing the assembly of bhikṣus to experience great evil dreams and become utterly terrified.
If one takes a celestial image and cleanses it with rice-gruel water, it will immediately return to its original state.
Then, having consecrated the aforementioned image once more,
bury it secretly within a cow pen.
This causes those oxen and other livestock to perceive a terrifying sign, so that they ultimately do not enter the pen.
Once the image has been removed, they return to their former state.
Furthermore, one may use the aforementioned image and suspend it from a wooden rack.
Below, use fire from buckwheat stalks to roast that celestial image while reciting the Great Mantra.
This causes all widowed women to give rise to reverence and love.
Furthermore, for the ritual of accomplishment:
use wood growing parasitically upon an auspicious fruit tree (*śrīphala*).
Fashion an image of the deity Pināyaka with two arms and three eyes,
inserting it within the horns of a bull;
then smear it with poisonous drugs, salt, mustard seeds, and the five kinds of amṛta medicines.
Wrap it in silk,
recite the Great Mantra to empower it, and bury it secretly before the door of a brothel;
then no people whatsoever will enter.
Furthermore, having consecrated the aforementioned image with mantras,
bury it secretly in front of a tavern; then,
not a single person will enter that tavern.
If one buries this divine image at the entrances of all types of shops,
such as oil and vinegar shops,
there will suddenly be no buyers or sellers, and no one will come at all.
If one removes the image of the deity, it will immediately return to its original state.
Furthermore, regarding the method for accomplishment:
fashion an image of the deity Pināyaka using a thorny wood stake.
Using poison, salt, mustard seeds, and the five kinds of ambrosial medicines, mix them together like clay and smear it upon that celestial image;
having recited the Great Mantra, one then uses a shroud from a corpse.
Above, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus flower with a celestial image placed within it;
having installed this beneath another person's house,
the vidyādhara does not return to his own place.
That person will quickly come to show respect and affection.
Furthermore, take the aforementioned image and wrap it in a shroud from a corpse;
then, using fire from *khadira* wood, heat the divine image while reciting the Great Mantra to empower it.
After a brief moment, a great wind and rain arise.
If one wishes to make them cease, one should bathe that image with *vajra* water and light a lamp of clarified butter;
it will immediately return to its former state.
Furthermore, one should take the aforementioned image and smear it with poison.
The vidyādhara, naked and with hair disheveled,
should suspend the divine image upon a wooden rack.
Having warmed it with a fire of wheat chaff,
one should drive khaṇḍirā wood stakes into the image of that deity,
while reciting the great mantra and uttering the person's name.
In a mere moment, that person will quickly arrive.
Whatever the practitioner desires to accomplish will be achieved.
Furthermore, one should use the aforementioned image and wool from a sheep to make a cord.
Tie it to the neck of that image.
The vidyādhara should pull the image with a rope while walking or sitting, reciting the person's name.
Recite the Great Mantra one hundred and eight times;
that person will swiftly contract a fever.
Furthermore, by roasting the image of that deity with fire for even a single period among the eight watches of the day, they will immediately meet their end.
Furthermore, using the aforementioned image and making a rope from *kuśa* grass,
one should tie that celestial image and suspend it beneath a wooden frame,
then roast that celestial image over heated oil.
Then, reciting the Great Mantra while calling out that person's name,
once a certain time has elapsed,
that person will swiftly become bound, and their body and mind will be seized with terror.
By washing the image with water, it immediately returns to its original state.
Furthermore, the practitioner of vidyā-mantras shall take the aforementioned image and use ox-bone to fashion a peg;
a hole is then made in the peg.
Place poisonous substances, mustard seeds, and a celestial image together inside a ritual stake.
Alternatively, when going out, tie it upon one's arm and recite the Great Mantra.
All who see him will be filled with joy.
If he enters a military array, the weapons of his adversaries shall become powerless.
In disputes and legal matters, when the principles of public justice are deliberated, he shall always prevail over others; even those who are inherently wicked will find delight upon seeing him.
Furthermore, for the accomplishment of the ritual application,
one should fashion an image of the deity Vināyaka using the root of the *sujana* tree,
and smear that image with a paste made of powdered black pepper.
Pour the juice of the *māla* wood and mustard oil into the mouth of the image.
Having heated it with a corpse-fire (*śavāgni*),
use the three pungent spices (*trikaṭu*), mustard salt, corpse-ash, *maṇḍala*, flowers, and fruit.
Mixing [the image] with mud like clay,
one should bury that image deep at a crossroads.
The vidyādhara should visualize the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka.
Assume the posture of the right dance.
Anoint your own left foot with mustard oil,
step upon the image, and recite this great vidyā-mantra:
Oṃ gṛtsi vidhṛtanānāmukagamarāya hūṃ. Having recited this great mantra, one then recites the following mantra:
Having recited this great mantra— Oṃ karūpa hūṃ phaṭ—
for seven days up to half a month, dispatch it;
that enemy will swiftly contract a grave illness and before long meet their end.
The Vidyādhara, exercising a mind of compassion,
extracts that image and restores it to its former state;
he then places the aforementioned image back inside the withered skull.
Having further filled it with poison,
he covered it with a dried skull and bound it with rope to suspend it from a wooden frame.
Below, one uses fire to scorch the image.
The Vidyādhara enters into the river and recites the Great Mantra (Mahāvidyā).
He then pours water from the aforementioned skull.
All the śatru-s and others shall either flee of their own accord or contract a grave illness;
they will all be utterly extinguished, leaving no trace behind.
Recite this great mantra:
Oṃ kāraṇudati hūṃ phaṭ. Having recited the mantra, the vidyādhara who applies himself with a sincere mind according to the ritual method will certainly attain accomplishment.
Alternatively, a vidyādhara may take the ashes from a fired clay vessel, smear them upon his own body,
wrap his head in a shroud from a corpse,
and enter the ocean or a great river.
Holding the aforementioned celestial image in the right hand and a rosary of human bones in the left hand,
one who recites the great mantra (*mahāvidyā*) ten million times shall become a lord of the earth.
Whether one desires to become a king or a military commander and so forth,
the practitioner of vidyā should again use the aforementioned image and fashion a ring from kuśa grass.
Place the image within the circle and sit again upon kuśa grass;
recite the Great Mantra one ayuta times.
One will attain the favor of the Rājakanyā or great wealth and status;
if she does not comply,
one should bind the image of that goddess with a cord of reed.
Boil some alkaline water and pour it over [the object].
The practitioner should visualize himself as the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka.
Then, the *dralha* (deity) will be struck with terror, and together with the previously mentioned *gaṇeya*, they will act according to the practitioner's intent.
If it has not yet been accomplished,
wrap the image of that deity in yellow wax and pin the image with a needle.
Heat the body of that image over a fire of khadira wood.
Within three days, the king and Kanyā will both obtain happiness.
Furthermore, the method for accomplishment:
Fashion an image of the deity Pināyaka out of tempered iron;
mix mustard oil with poison to form a paste like clay,
and smear it upon that image of the deity.
Using tongs, one should hold the image over a fire of dry wood and roast it while reciting the Great Mantra,
causing that hostile person to contract a severe illness.
If a vidyādhara takes an image of a deity to another house and returns to his own house after a brief moment,
he shall perform worship there for the duration of one day.
By means of this mantra, summon that person to quickly appear before you;
serve and provide for them with everything according to their wishes.
Furthermore, the method for accomplishment is as follows:
Using *kumārī* clay, one fashions an image of the deity Pināyaka.
When the vidyādhara places it upon his pillow and sleeps,
all matters concerning cities, districts, villages, and their past, future, and present events [will be revealed].
One can explain all of this.
If a vidyādhara holds an image in his hand and enters a great military array,
he cannot be harmed by spears, swords, weapons, or any such implements.
Even all evil persons will be unable to harm them.
Furthermore, one should place the aforementioned image within the ashes of the corpse;
the vidyādhara [should then] use vajra-water.
Having sprinkled water for purification upon one's own body and having drunk that water, one should immediately recite this great vidyā-mantra:
Oṃ kararupe hūṃ phaṭ. Having recited this great vidyā-mantra, one should also state the matter for which one seeks.
At that time, all the people of that village will have their minds deranged;
like those afflicted by wind-demons, they will be utterly unable to distinguish between good and evil.
If the mantra-adept extracts that image from there, [the calamity shall cease].
It will immediately become as it was before.
Furthermore, for the method of accomplishment:
use *sāṃvartana* wood.
He forms the image of the deity Pināyaka,
with twelve arms and four feet,
holding various weapons and implements in his hands.
Wearing a garment made of the skin of a *kṛtānala* insect,
he bites his lips with his teeth to assume a most fierce appearance.
Having assumed this form, he offers beef from a water buffalo into the corpse-fire while reciting the Great Mantra.
Having performed the homa ten thousand times,
the vidyādhara shall consume the five kinds of nectar-medicines and smear them upon his own body; then,
holding wine in his left hand, he should proceed.
Holding water and beef in the right hand,
visualize oneself as the Vidyārāja Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
He stood with his feet together, fully endowed with all the marks [of a great man],
and with a sharp sword he severed that image;
immediately, the bodies of Setukṛ and the others were all split in two.
This method of accomplishment can also, at the site of a battle,
manifest in a dream to harmoniously exhort the parties to quickly cease their strife.
Furthermore, one should employ the aforementioned image.
The Vidyādhara binds the left foot of the image with a cord and suspends it beneath a wooden frame while reciting the Great Mantra.
In this way, he can subdue Śatru-s and others according to the practitioner’s will. If one wishes to release the previous form, the image returns to its original state.
Furthermore, take the aforementioned image and bind it with iron chains;
bury it secretly before the gate of the king’s palace.
Then all the servants and attendants of that residence will be as if bound by ropes, unable to move.
Upon removing that image, it will immediately return to its original state.
Furthermore, for the method of accomplishment:
use wood growing parasitically upon a Bodhi tree.
One should fashion an image of the deity Pināyaka,
eight finger-widths in height, with four arms, three eyes, and a crown upon his head;
his first right hand holds a vajra.
The second hand holds a rosary;
the first left hand touches a nāga,
and the second left hand grasps a khaṭvāṅga.
Having fashioned this image,
one should construct a square maṇḍala using cow dung;
within the maṇḍala, one should place the divine image with its face covered.
The Vidyādhara should tread upon the image with his left foot and recite the Great Mantra three times each day.
When one month has passed, he should again take the divine image and place it within a storehouse.
This will cause the storehouses and treasuries to become filled with wealth and jewels.
Furthermore, one should step upon the image with the left foot while reciting the mantra while calling out the name.
One will attain an inexhaustible treasury to enjoy throughout all time, never lacking anything.
If one does not wish to use it for treading upon others to cause calamity,
the Vidyādhara should address the image, saying:
"If you do not rely upon my teaching,
I shall cause the great vajra-pestle of the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka to shatter your head.
Having spoken thus, he continued:
Furthermore, within the treasury, one should perform offerings according to the ritual with *argha*, incense, flowers, and so forth, three times each day.
Then, one addresses the image, saying: "Cease your abiding in samādhi."
Just as one cannot escape the fire at the end of an eon,
having spoken thus, the practitioner takes this divine image and goes to a field or a threshing floor of grain and barley.
Even when one arrives at places such as markets and shops,
if one constantly recollects the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka,
all wealth and treasures will be abundantly sufficient, and one shall enjoy them without end.
Furthermore, using the aforementioned image,
if the vidyādhara maintains it throughout his lifetime and travels to various cities,
towns, and villages, [he shall achieve success].
Even when traveling by boat upon rivers and seas to conduct business and seek profit, one shall obtain double the wealth and gain;
free from all obstacles and difficulties, everything shall accord with one's wishes.
Upon returning to one's original home, one should constantly offer incense, flowers, food, and drink.
One should perform offerings such as argha according to the ritual rules,
protecting and honoring [the deity] like one's own parents;
if one fails to offer worship and respect, calamities will surely arise.
Again, use the previous image;
tie it with rope and suspend it from a wooden frame,
then heat it from below using a fire of bean-pods.
The Vidyādhara, naked and with disheveled hair,
assuming a form of great wrath, strikes the image with a cord of hair;
the desired objective will certainly be accomplished.
Furthermore, using the aforementioned image and parched barley, roast it over a fire.
From that time forward, day by day, one will be able to obtain food and drink of the finest quality,
such that all one's retinue shall be fully satisfied.
If one does not act according to these instructions, calamities will surely arise,
and one will transgress the methods for accomplishing samādhi.
Furthermore, regarding the methods for accomplishment:
The Vidyādhara should fashion an image of that deity from khadira wood;
it should be ten fingers in height and possess twelve arms,
holding various weapons and standing in a dancing posture.
Holding *suramasa* in both hands,
having performed this,
the vidyādhara proceeds to the śmaśāna.
Either within an empty house or inside a temple of Maheśvara,
one should step upon the image of that deity with the left foot and recite the Great Mantra three times each day.
Oṃ hṛtsidhri vikṛtānana amukam samāraya mādaya śoṣaya ucchādaya grāsa grāsaya oṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. The vidyādhara recites this great mantra.
If one consecrates a divine image for three full months,
all obstacles (*sthūla*) beyond a range of one hundred *yojanas* will be swiftly eliminated.
Thus, the practitioner of the vidyā-mantra achieves accomplishment.
Again, use the aforementioned image,
along with poisonous substances, mustard seeds,
salt, and mandārava seeds.
Mix it together like clay and smear it upon the body of the image.
The Vidyādhara should smear his own body with the ashes of a corpse and drink a small amount of alcohol.
One assumes the form of the Wrathful Vidyārāja, manifesting the aspect of great fearlessness.
One joins two pieces of blue stone together within the stone image;
the practitioner then abides in their body as the Vidyārāja Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
If one recites the Great Mantra for a full three months,
all *śatru*s and others,
even those possessing the power of Śakra, must perish.
Furthermore, using the aforementioned image, tie it around the neck of that [target] image with a woolen cord;
having covered the head and eyes of the image with an object and veiled its face,
bury it within the ashes of a corpse.
While reciting the great mantra and invoking the name of Śatru,
the vidyādhara should visualize himself as the Vidyārāja Yamāntaka standing before the image.
In an instant, all the inhabitants of the four great continents became silent as if mute;
they closed their eyes and could see nothing at all.
Even if evil persons from as far as Rāṣṭra were to kill one's wife and children,
they would not be able to speak, as if they were bound and restrained.
